Images varied in size and subtended areas from 31.0 × 38.5 degrees of visual angle (°) to 56.9°× 50.1°. Example Chest Radiograph Images Note. Sample chest radiographs for the detection and eye-tracking task. The right side of the images correspond to the left side of the body. Images contained (A) a single subtle abnormality (right upper zone lesion), (B) no abnormalities (normal), (C) a single obvious abnormality (left upper zone mass), and (D) multiple abnormalities (right middle zone lesion and right pneumothorax). A B were manifestations of various diseases including adenocarcinoma, metastasis, sarcoidosis, chronic lung allograft dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, and tuberculosis. Abnormalities were defined within an area of interest (AOI) using EyeLink Data Viewer. Axis-aligned rectangular regions were drawn manually around each abnormality within an image. Each AOI was specified in screen-pixel coordinates by its left, top, right, and bottom boundaries. Pixels areas covered by each AOI varied across images, reflecting differences in lesion size and spatial extent (e.g., more diffuse abnormalities such as lobar atelectasis or extensive consolidation were enclosed in larger rectangles).

Apparatus

Stimuli were presented on a 21.5" Dell P2217H LCD monitor (brightness 250 cd/m 2 ) with a 1920 × 1200 resolution and 60 Hz refresh rate using MATLAB with Psychophysics toolbox (Brainard, 1997) at a viewing distance of approximately 80 cm. Eye movements were tracked monocularly using the Eyelink Portable Duo (SR Research) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz in a remote unrestrained mode. The eye tracker was mounted on a tripod and placed approximately 55 cm from the participant's eyes and was controlled with the Eyelink Host PC (Dell Latitude 5420 Core i5 11 th Gen) and Eyelink toolbox in MATLAB (Cornelissen et al., 2002).

Procedure

Pre-and post-testing data was collected on the Academy campus in a low-lit room that resembled a typical reporting environment. Participants were seated in front of the monitor and eye tracker, and a verbal explanation of the task was given. Participants were instructed to view each image and identify abnormalities as accurately as possible using a mouse click. Participants were told that images could contain no abnormalities, a single abnormality, or multiple abnormalities, but they were not made aware of the prevalence of abnormalities across the images (approximately 80%). Participants were instructed that there was no time limit but that they should aim to spend no longer than one minute on each image and indicate the end of their search with a spacebar press. A target sticker was placed on the forehead above the eyebrow of the tracked eye to enable head position tracking. This was followed by a standard 9-point calibration procedure. The calibration was accepted if the average error was below 0.5° and the maximum error was no larger than 1.2°. Before the task began, participants were reminded to maintain a stable viewing distance and minimize head movement. Between each trial a fixation cross appeared in the center of the screen.

Participants confirmed their fixation and readiness to proceed to the next trial by pressing the spacebar. If a spatial mismatch between the recorded and actual gaze positions was observed between trials, a drift correction was applied. The task took approximately 45 minutes to complete in total. In the pre-test session, the task was followed by a brief demographic questionnaire. Approximately one week later, participants attended the two-day CXR interpretation course. Upon completing the course, they returned for the post-test session, which followed the same procedure as the pre-test using the alternative image bank.

Results

Deviations from preregistration

Planned measurements, data exclusions and analyses deviated from the preregistration in the following ways: 1.

We initially planned to assess accuracy for abnormal cases as the proportion of images where all abnormalities were identified and no false positive identifications were made. In practice, participants showed a high false alarm rate meaning very few trials met this criterion. To obtain more informative indices of performance we instead considered cases to be accurate if all abnormalities had been correctly identified irrespective of any additional false positive marks.

2. We planned to categorize misses into scanning, recognition, and decision-making errors using a 260 millisecond (ms) fixation duration threshold, based on work using a simplified multiple-target search task (Cain et al., 2013). However, the radiology literature suggests this value is not appropriate for our CXR stimuli, where recognition of abnormalities require longer dwell times. We therefore revised the threshold to a dwell time of 600 ms in line with the error taxonomy of prior work in radiology (Kundel et al., 1978).

3. There were a few instances in which participants expressed to the researcher that they had accidentally terminated the trial before they had finished searching, and these trials were removed from all performance and eye movement analyses since they did not reflect valid performance (n = 4).

4. Although participants were instructed to avoid head movement as much as possible, inspection of the eye-tracking data during preprocessing indicated a small number of trials were affected by head motion leading to unstable or missing gaze estimates. To identify trials with unstable tracking, we examined the mean saccade duration per trial; trials with an average saccade duration exceeding 200 ms were taken to reflect pronounced tracking drift and were excluded from all eye movement analyses. This criterion was applied uniformly across participants and sessions and resulted in the removal of only a small proportion of trials overall (<1%).

5. We originally planned to conduct a 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with session (pre, post) and subtlety (subtle, obvious) as within-participant factors. However, subtle, obvious and multiple-target images each represent three distinct levels of difficulty and diagnostic complexity in our stimulus set. Since training effects might reasonably differ across the full range of abnormal cases, we revised the subtlety factor to case type (subtle, obvious, multiple), resulting in a 2 × 3 repeated measures ANOVA.

Training outcome measures

To assess the impact of training, we calculated several performance measures within the pre-and post-test data. For abnormal cases, accurate detection was defined as correctly identifying all abnormalities present (single subtle, single obvious, multiple) irrespective of any additional false positive markings. Accuracy rates for abnormal images were therefore calculated as the proportion of correct cases divided by total number of cases for each case type separately (subtle accuracy, obvious accuracy, multiple-target accuracy). As an additional index of multiple-target accuracy, we calculated subsequent-target accuracy (proportion of additional abnormalities detected given at least one abnormality had been found). The correct rejection rate was calculated as the proportion of images correctly identified as normal with no false positives, and the proportion of abnormal images with at least one false positive reflected the false alarm rate. Total search time was measured as the time elapsed between stimulus onset and trial termination (spacebar press) in seconds (s).

Eye-movement measures

To examine search behavior, we extracted several eye-movement metrics within each testing phase. Fixation and saccadic events were classified using EyeLink's default velocity

Categorization of misses

All missed abnormalities across all abnormal images were categorized according to the fixation data (Carmody et al., 1980; Kundel et al., 1978; Samuel et al., 1995). If an abnormality was never fixated, it was classified as a scanning error. If an abnormality was fixated but the total dwell time was less than 600 ms, it was categorized as a recognition error. Missed abnormalities with dwell times more than 600 ms were classified as decisionmaking errors. We calculated the counts of each error type across the pre-and post-test sessions as well as their proportions.

Planned analyses

We report both traditional frequentist statistics using p-values and Bayesian statistics using Bayes factors. Frequentist significance was assessed using an alpha level of .05. To evaluate the strength of the evidence, Bayes factors were computed using the Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) prior (r = .707; Rouder et al., 2009) in JASP (JASP Team, 2025).

Accordingly, a BF10 > 6 was considered evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis over the null, whereas a BF10 < .17 was interpreted as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis over the alternative hypothesis (Wagenmakers et al., 2018). For our inferential statistics, where relevant, tests of sphericity were carried out using Mauchly's test. In cases where sphericity was violated, we report the Greenhouse-Geisser-corrected degrees of freedom and p-values.

Equivalence of difficulty across data banks

Before examining training effects, we assessed whether the two stimulus banks differed in difficulty across abnormal image types at baseline using a mixed 2 x 3 ANOVA with stimulus bank (A, B) as a between-participant factor and case type (subtle, obvious, multiple) as a within-participant factor. The analysis revealed a significant main effect of case type (F(1.40, 16.85) = 230.91, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.95, BF10 = 2.38×10 19 ), as expected, with obvious abnormalities identified more accurately than subtle (t(12) = 25.08, p <.001, d = 6.58, BF10 = 2.06×10 9 ) or multiple abnormalities (t(12) = 20.62, p < .001, d = 6.70, BF10 = 1.00×10 8 ). There was no significant main effect of stimulus bank (F(1, 12) = 1.92, p = 0.191, η²ₚ = 0.14, BF10 = 0.38) and no significant stimulus bank × trial type interaction (F(1.40, 16.85) = 1.39, p = 0.267, η²ₚ = 0.10, BF10 = 0.62), indicating no evidence that the two image banks differed at baseline.

Impact of training on detection accuracy and search times

Differences in detection accuracy for subtle, obvious and multiple abnormalities across the pre-and post-testing phases were assessed with a 2 × 3 repeated measures ANOVA with time (pre, post) and case type (subtle, obvious, multiple) as within-participant factors. The repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of time (F(1, 13) = 5.07, p = .042, η²ₚ = .28, BF10 = 1.71; Figure 2) where accuracy at detecting abnormalities improved post-test relative to pre-test collapsed across case type (t(13) = 2.25, p = .042, d = 0.54, BF10 = 4.86). There was also a significant main effect of case type (F(1.31, 16.98) = 474.26, p < .001, η²ₚ = .97, BF10 = 2.45×10 18 ), where accuracy at identifying obvious abnormalities was significantly higher than accuracy at identifying subtle abnormalities (t(13) = 32.35, p < .001, d = 6.26, BF10 = 4.17×10 20 ) and all abnormalities in images with multiple targets (t(13) = 34.96, p < .001, d = 6.42, BF10 = 2.16×10 19 ) across both testing phases. There were no differences in accuracy between subtle and multiple-target cases collapsed across the pre-and post-test (t(13) = 0.53, p = .526, d = 0.16, BF10 = 0.24) suggesting that initial abnormality detection did not affect subsequent abnormality detection. The time × case type interaction was not significant (F(2, 26) = 0.18, p = .834, η²ₚ = .01, BF10 = 0.21). Despite small improvements in detection accuracy, the false alarm rate across abnormal images was consistent across both testing phases (t(13) = 0.33, p = .751, d = 0.09, BF10 = 0.28; Table 1), and the tendency to report false positive findings in normal images also remained consistent as reflected in the correct rejection rate (t(13) = 1.17, p = .265, d = 0.31, BF10 = 0.48). Further paired samples t-tests did not indicate significant changes in the proportion of additional abnormalities found after an initial abnormal finding was identified (t(13) = 0.43, p = .677, d = 0.11, BF10 = 0.29) from pre-to post-test. The total time searching each image also did not change significantly from pre-to post-test (t(13) = 1.06, p = .307, d = 0.28, BF10 = 0.44).

Impact of training on oculomotor behavior 491

Table 2 reports the descriptive statistics for our eye movement measures before and 492 after training. To assess the impact of training on our primary eye movement measures, we 493 performed one-tailed paired samples t-tests across the pre-and post-test phases. There were 494 no significant changes in fixation counts (t(13) = 1.40, p = .093, d = 0.38, BF+0 = 1.08), time 495 to first fixate on an abnormality (t(13) = 0.58, p = .287, d = 0.15, BF+0 = 0.44), fixation 496 durations (t(13) = 1.56, p = .929, d = 0.42, BF+0 = 0.12), saccade amplitudes (t(13) = 1.58, p497 = .931, d = 0.42, BF-0 = 0.12), or the dwell time on an abnormality (t(13) = 0.60, p = .720, d = 498 0.16, BF-0 = 0.18). Two-tailed paired samples t-tests across the pre-and post-test phases also 499 revealed no significant changes in the saccade rate (t(13) = 1.27, p = .228, d = 0.34, BF10 = 500 0.53), saccade duration (t(13) = 0.85, p = .411, d = 0.23, BF10 = 0.37), or the time to first 501 initiate an eye movement (t(13) = 0.80, p = .437, d = 0.22, BF10 = 0.36). 502

Impact of training on types of miss errors 506

Although there were small improvements in accuracy overall, miss errors remained 507 prevalent (see Figure 3). To assess the causes of these errors and examine whether the 508 relative counts of each error type changed following training, a 2 × 3 repeated-measures 509 ANOVA with time (pre, post) and error type (scanning, recognition, decision-making) as 510 within-participant factors was conducted. Analyses revealed a significant main effect of time 511 (F(1, 13) = 5.62, p = .034, η²ₚ = 0.30, BF10 = 0.27), where the total number of miss errors 512 were reduced in the post-test (t(13) = 2.37, p = .034, d = 0.26, BF10 = 0.17), however, there 513 was anecdotal evidence in favor of the null suggesting evidence for a true difference is not 514 robust. There was no significant time × error type interaction (F(1.25, 16.31) = 0.77, p515 = .423, η²ₚ = 0.06, BF10 = 0.36). However, the main effect of error type was significant 516 (F(1.12, 14.59) = 24.35, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.65, BF10 = 4.97×10 3 ), and post-hoc tests showed 517 that the number of decision-making errors was significantly larger than both recognition 518 errors (t(13) = 6.25, p < .001, d = 2.03, BF10 = 1.13×10 4 ) and scanning errors (t(13) = 4.29, p519 = .002, d = 1.81, BF10 = 219.50), and that scanning and recognition errors occurred at a 520 similar frequency (t(13) = 1.45, p = .170, d = 0.22, BF10 = 0.75). 521 Error Type Counts Before and After Training Note. Violin plots represent data distribution of counts of scanning, recognition and decisionmaking errors. Box plots represent the interquartile range, minimum value, and maximum value. Errors bars for mean scores are ± the standard error.

On average across the pre-and post-test sessions, decision-making errors made up the largest proportion of misses (M = .51, SD = .13), with scanning errors (M = .26, SD = .09) and recognition errors (M = .23, SD = .05) occurring at similar rates. However, these averages mask considerable variability among the trainees. Although for most trainees' errors were dominated by faulty decision-making, for others incomplete scanning and failures to recognize suspicious regions were the dominant causes (see Figure 4).

Exploratory analyses

Categorization of subtle omissions and subsequent search misses

We additionally explored whether the types of errors differed according to whether the missed abnormality followed the detection of an initial finding (Samuel et al., 1995). We compared missed subtle cases to multiple-target cases where at least one abnormality had been correctly identified but the remaining abnormalities were missed (SSM) among the posttest data. Since there were more subtle cases than multiple-target cases, we focused our analysis on the relative proportion of error types. A 2 × 3 repeated measures ANOVA with case type (subtle, SSM) and error type (scanning, recognition, decision-making) as withinparticipant factors revealed no significant main effect of case type (F(1, 13) = 0.003, p = .960, η²ₚ = 2.04×10 -4 , BF10 = 0.28; Figure 5) and no significant trial type × error type interaction (F(2, 26) = 0.07, p = .935, η²ₚ = 0.01, BF10 = 0.21). The main effect of error type was significant (F(1.20, 15.65) = 9.38, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.42, BF10 = 44.47), and post-hoc analyses revealed a significantly higher proportion of decision-making errors compared to scanning errors (t(13) = 2.89, p = .042, d = 1.32, BF10 = 18.41) and recognition errors (t(13) = 4.08, p = .004, d = 1.53, BF10 = 221.20) across both trial types, but no significant differences in the proportion of scanning errors and recognition errors (t(13) = 0.98, p = .350, d = 0.21, BF10 = 0.31). Error Type Proportions for Missed Subtle and Subsequent Abnormalities Note. Violin plots represent data distribution of proportions of scanning, recognition and decision-making errors. Box plots represent the interquartile range, minimum value, and maximum value. Errors bars for mean scores are ± the standard error.

Reliability checks

We further examined reliability of our key performance and eye-movement metrics across the pre-and post-test using the intraclass correlation coefficient 1 (ICC; see Figure 6).

Reliability estimates varied substantially, ranging from poor to excellent (Cicchetti & Sparrow, 1981; Landis & Koch, 1977). Accuracy measures and target-specific eye-movement measures generally showed poor-to-moderate stability (ICC < 0.6), but several global eyemovement metrics exceeded good (.6 ≤ ICC < .8) and excellent ranges (ICC ≥ .8), along with the correct rejection rate (ICC = 0.81; Figure 6). This pattern suggests individual global differences in gaze behavior and correct rejection rates were relatively stable over time, whereas case-level performance measures were more sensitive to session-specific factors.

1 A two-way mixed-effects model for absolute agreement was used where the ICC value represents the proportion of total variance attributable to differences between participants whilst accounting for measurement and error variance (Koo & Li, 2016). Variance Components for Performance and Eye Movement Measures Note. Each bar equates the total variance for a given measure, and each variance component is represented by a light blue bar (error variance), a light pink bar (between-participant variance) and a dark pink bar (between-session variance). Intraclass correlation coefficients are shown inside the base of the light blue bar.

Discussion

The purpose of this study was to examine whether a two-day CXR interpretation course could improve abnormality detection, enhance search pattern efficiency, and alter the distribution of error types in first-year radiology trainees. Following training, there were small improvements in detection accuracy overall. Performance for subtle abnormalities and images containing multiple abnormalities remained poor, and false-positive rates were persistent on over half of the normal and abnormal images, a pattern which is typical of radiologists at the very earliest stages of their training. Contrary to expectations, training did not produce meaningful shifts in eye-movement metrics typically associated with expert-like scanning. Across both testing phases, most missed abnormalities (75%) had been fixated at least once, with approximately one quarter of misses attributable to incomplete scanning.

Among the fixated misses, over a quarter reflected failures of recognition and over half were cases in which trainees recognized the region as potentially abnormal but ultimately judged it to be normal, indicating that faulty decision-making was the predominant source of error.

In line with previous studies, our results demonstrated a small improvement in detecting abnormalities in CXR among first-year radiology trainees following completion of a two-day CXR interpretation course focus on anatomical and pathological content (Hegazi et al., 2025; Wentzell et al., 2018), although our Bayesian analyses provided only anecdotal evidence for this effect suggesting a larger sample size is needed to definitively determine training effects. Nevertheless, trainees were far superior at identifying obvious abnormalities reaching almost ceiling performance, compared to subtle abnormalities and more complex cases with multiple abnormalities. Although there were small improvements in detection accuracy overall, performance for subtle and multiple-target cases remained below 30%. These persistent errors may arise because first-year radiology trainees lack a fully systematic approach to viewing, so abnormalities that are not salient, appear in "blind spots", or are followed by identification of an initial highly salient abnormality may not come into foveal view (del Ciello et al., 2017; Gefter et al., 2023; Gefter & Hatabu, 2023). Additionally, trainees may show deficits in recognition or decision-making regarding the problem region once it has been fixated because they lack the knowledge and experience needed to correctly encode abnormal features or discriminate them from normal variants (Norman, 2005; van der Gijp et al., 2014). These accounts are not mutually exclusive, but understanding the distribution of the causes of miss errors can offer guidance in terms of where training should be targeted.

Our results suggest that poorer performance among trainees was driven predominantly by recognition-or decision-making deficits, which is consistent with previous work (Kundel et al., 1978). Of the fixated abnormalities, 31% were not recognized and 69% were actively judged to be normal, and this pattern held for both cases of missed subtle abnormalities and missed abnormalities that followed detection of an initial abnormality. In line with this latter finding, we did not observe differences in detection rates for subtle abnormalities in contrast to finding all abnormalities in multiple-target cases, contrary to most of the literature on the cost searching for multiple targets (Berbaum et al., 1998 (Berbaum et al., , 2015;; Cain & Mitroff, 2012; Cain et al., 2013; Samuel et al., 1995). One important consideration is that our cohort consisted of radiologists at the very beginning of their training, whereas much of the existing literature has focused on more experienced radiologists, limiting the extent to which multiple-target costs would be observed. Additionally, trainees spent roughly half a minute searching each case which is substantially below the permitted one minute indicating that they adopted relatively rapid search strategies. This search regime and generally poor performance on subtle cases, together with our lack of tight control over the relative salience of first and subsequent findings, may have limited the extent to which subtle differences between single-and multiple-target search could emerge. Since both viewing time and target salience are known to modulate the SSM effect (e.g., Berbaum et al., 1990 Berbaum et al., , 1991;; Fleck et al., 2010), we cannot rule out SSM-like mechanisms entirely.

We observed enhanced sensitivity of abnormalities among trainees following training, and false-positive rates in both abnormal and normal images remained unchanged, similar to previous work (Hegazi et al., 2025; Wentzell et al., 2018). This pattern suggests that training primarily improved detection and recognition processes rather than inducing a liberal shift in global decision criterion; trainees were more likely to correctly identify present abnormalities without a corresponding increase in over-calling normal findings as abnormal (Wolfe et al., 2016). In the earliest stages of training, discriminating normal anatomy from abnormal can be difficult as trainees have not yet encountered the full spectrum of normal anatomical variations resulting in unfamiliar features being misinterpreted as pathological (Abbott, 2025; Fabre et al., 2018). These latter findings have clear implications for training; whereby there should be more emphasis on interpreting normal films and their variants. Training generally focuses on abnormal images where a large amount of anatomy and pathology needs to be covered, but this does not reflect what happens in practice where the prevalence of disease can be low, such as screening for lung cancer (Bhartia et al., 2024). Manipulating the ratios of abnormal to normal cases in training can influence learning and performance outcomes where students who are trained with mostly abnormal images are less likely to miss abnormalities and students training with mostly normal images are less likely to report abnormalities that are not present (Pusic et al., 2012; van Geel et al., 2019). Training programs should therefore ensure to implement both normal and abnormal cases to improve pattern recognition and develop robust decision-making skills among trainees to reduce both misses and false positives in practice (van der Gijp et al., 2014).

Although false-positive errors were common amongst trainees, it is arguably the misses that warrant closer attention, given their greater potential for harm. Approximately one quarter of misses were scanning failures, and training did not markedly reduce the number of these scanning errors. Consistent with this, we found no compelling evidence that the training course altered trainees' gaze behavior. Abnormality-specific indices (time to first fixate on an abnormality, dwell time) and other global spatial-temporal dynamics (saccade amplitude, saccade duration, saccade rate, initiation time, fixation duration and count) showed no significant changes after training, with several Bayes factors providing at most anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis. Our observed patterns of trainee scanning behavior differ from findings that suggest EMMEs or repetitive exposure to a pathology detection task with feedback can lead novices to adopt more expert-like scan paths (Brams et al., 2021; Litchfield et al., 2010; McLaughlin et al., 2021). One possibility is that the apparent impact of EMMEs on eye movements in prior work (e.g., Litchfield et al., 2010; McLaughlin et al., 2021) is overestimated because control conditions often lacked equivalent immediate feedback on lesion location, a critical driver of perceptual learning (Sha et al., 2020). Another possibility is that training focused on a relatively narrow set of focal pathologies (e.g., lung nodules and focal consolidations) over more extended periods of time (Brams et al., 2021). This latter design may therefore have been more powerful in reshaping scanning and enhancing performance for a specific class of abnormalities, while our intervention was geared towards building more general interpretive competence across a wider range of findings. Furthermore, our sample only had sufficient sensitivity to detect large effect sizes which may have limited our ability to detect subtle changes in oculomotor behaviour. While our present findings provide little evidence that training produces large shifts in visual search behaviour, smaller but potentially meaningful changes cannot be ruled out.

Taken together, our findings point to a dissociation between search-related processes and later recognition and decision-making processes in early CXR training. In our sample, over half of the abnormalities omitted were decision-making errors, and although the relative proportion of decision-making errors did not decrease, overall accuracy improved while scanning errors remained stable. Early gains in expertise therefore appear to be driven more by strengthened internal representations of what is normal or abnormal and sharpened decision criteria applied to fixated features (Hegazi et al., 2025; Wentzell et al., 2018), rather than by restructuring of oculomotor strategies. This interpretation differs somewhat from prior work which reports that expert-like search patterns emerged earlier than expert diagnostic performance (Kelly et al., 2016). However, an important distinction here is that our task primarily focused on the detection and localization of abnormalities rather than formal image interpretation. As such, it is possible that expert-like search behaviour may develop before expert diagnostic reasoning (Kelly et al., 2016), while improvements in abnormality detection among novices can occur independently of measurable changes in search strategy. Current theoretical accounts of perceptual expertise in medical image perception emphasize the gradual tuning of target templates and categorical decision-making as radiologists gain experience and are exposed to more variant cases, with efficient and differentiated search patterns emerging as these perceptual skills become established (Brunyé et al., 2019; Gegenfurtner et al., 2011; Waite et al., 2019 Waite et al., , 2020)). Within broader theoretical frameworks of visual search, our findings are consistent with the idea that medical image perception is largely dependent on top-down guidance, that is, knowledge of normal and abnormal anatomy, expectations about locations abnormalities are likely to be, and learned associations between subtle features and diagnoses (Wolfe et al., 2016; Wolfe & Horowitz, 2017). Further work following trainees as they progress through training milestones is needed to clarify how eye movement patterns develop as knowledge is acquired and how these changes relate to perceptual learning and diagnostic accuracy, respectively (Papesh et al., 2021; Sowden et al., 2000; Sunday et al., 2017).

Our data suggests CXR education should prioritize practical training that sharpens discrimination between normal variants and pathology and gives trainees deliberate practice interpreting subtle and multi-lesion cases. Recent work shows that computer-based perceptual training (repeated discrimination of normal and abnormal cases with immediate feedback) can improve nodule detection on CXR images (Alexander et al., 2020; Auffermann et al., 2015; Sha et al., 2020), including when AI-augmented images are used to expand training sets and reduce faculty workload in producing data banks (Borgbjerg et al., 2023; Tajmir & Alkasab, 2018). Such interventions may help accelerate the acquisition of expertise, consistent with the view that effective search patterns emerge as trainees develop robust knowledge of where abnormalities tend to occur and how normal and abnormal features appear (Kundel & La Follette, 1972). Systematic or checklist approaches may still be useful as scaffolds, especially for trainees who do not know where to start (Sethole et al., 2023), but these should supplement, rather than replace, training that focus on pattern recognition and decision-making processes. One important caveat to recognize, however, is that a "one-sizefits-all" training model may not address the specific needs of individual trainees. Although for most trainees, misses were dominated by faulty decision-making, a minority were driven primarily by incomplete scanning, emphasizing the need to identify these individuals and tailor training processes accordingly (Kellman & Krasne, 2018; Waite et al., 2019 Waite et al., , 2020). An additional consideration for training is the increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond supporting more efficient image interpretation (Plesner et al., 2023), AI may have a future role in education and competency assessment by helping identify individual learning needs and monitor progression. However, it remains essential that trainees and trainers develop the skills required to critically evaluate and appropriately use AI outputs in clinical practice (Agarwal et al., 2024).

Additional methods such as eye-tracking may have a role in competency assessments by revealing individual differences in search behavior, but currently there is no universal marker of optimal diagnostic performance and any use in assessment will require careful validation and interpretation (Kok, 2019; Waite et al., 2020). Our exploratory reliability analyses indicated that only a subset of global eye-tracking metrics emerged as promising candidates for capturing individual differences in search behavior. Fixation duration, saccade rate and initiation time showed excellent reliability, suggesting that these aspects of oculomotor control are relatively stable within observers, although how these relate to diagnostic accuracy was beyond the scope of the current study. At the decision-making level, correct-rejection rates for normal cases also showed excellent reliability, indicating that the tendency to accurately dismiss normal images is a robust characteristic of individual performance and could be levered in future work on tailored training and competency evaluation (Layher et al., 2020).

There are several limitations that should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, we used localization as a proxy of what trainees considered to be abnormal without asking for explicit diagnostic labels (Kok et al., 2016). This approach captures where trainees directed overt attention and which regions they judged as abnormal, but it does not reveal how they would have described or prioritized those findings in a formal report, limiting inferences about interpretive accuracy (Alexander et al., 2020; Krupinski, 2010).

Second, trainees viewed each image without clinical history which typically offers guidance in prioritizing differential diagnoses (Hegazi et al., 2025), and were not able to interact with the display which may have affected their ability to perceive more subtle cases findings (Zenger et al., 2025). Given these limitations, it is unclear how closely task performance maps onto real-world reporting competence in the clinical environment. Our study also lacked a concurrent control group, making it difficult to disentangle improvements attributable specifically to the CXR course from those arising from familiarity with the task.

In addition, the sample comprised a relatively small cohort of first-year trainees from a single training academy, which may constrain statistical power to detect subtle changes in eye movements and limit the generalizability to other programs or training levels. Future work should explore the impact of different CXR training formats in large multi-center cohorts with appropriate control conditions.

Summary and conclusion

Our findings suggest that a short CXR interpretation course can produce small gains in detection of abnormalities among first-year radiology trainees. Importantly, the primary benefit of the course may be in providing a structured framework for strengthening trainees' ability to distinguish normal from abnormal appearances, rather than globally altering visual search. The main barriers to expert performance lie in discriminating subtle pathology from normal variants and in decisional processes, rather than in gross failures of search, an observation that has important implications for the design and evaluation of future teaching and training. Our findings further suggest that different components of radiological expertise may develop at different rates, with early improvements emerging in detection and discrimination before measurable changes in visual search behaviour. These early gains are likely underpinned by the gradual development of anatomical-pathological schemas and may be accelerated through perceptual learning paradigms and AI-assisted educational tools.

However, there was considerable variability between trainees, where error was dominated by incomplete searching for some individuals and pattern recognition or faulty decision-making for others, highlighting the need for competency assessments that identify individual weaknesses and support tailored training approaches.

Event samples that fell outside the bounds of the image being presented were removed and trials that were contaminated by tracking drifts/loss because of head movement were also excluded from any aggregate eye movement computations (see Deviations from preregistration). Across all images we calculated the average number of fixations (fixation count), the average length of time (ms) the eyes remained still between saccades (fixation duration), the average distance (°) of eye movements (saccade amplitude), the average time elapsed from stimulus onset to the first fixation (s) on an abnormality (time to first fixate), and the total average time spent fixating (s) on an abnormality (dwell time). Further measures included the average number of eye movements made to new locations per second (saccade rate), the average latency of eye movements (saccade duration), and the time elapsed (ms) between stimulus onset and the first eye movement (initiation time).
